holidays.name: Put On Your Own Shoes Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate independence, one lace, buckle, and Velcro strap at a time. Little ones are encouraged to wrestle their own footwear on, even if the left shoe ends up on the right foot. Grown-ups get to practice patience while the toddler works it out.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance of unclear origin. It has become a favorite in parenting and preschool circles as a nudge toward self-sufficiency.
holidays.funFact: Toddlers often master pulling on shoes well before they can tie laces. Many kids don't learn to tie laces until around age five or six, which is why Velcro became a parenting hero.

holidays.name: National Gazpacho Day
holidays.description: A salute to the chilled Spanish soup that proves soup can be refreshing, even in December. Tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers, garlic, and olive oil are blended into a vibrant, zesty bowl. It is a very cold way to mark a very cold month.
holidays.origin: Gazpacho comes from southern Spain, specifically Andalusia, where it began as a humble mix of bread, garlic, olive oil, and vinegar. The day itself is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin.
holidays.funFact: The original gazpacho had no tomatoes. Tomatoes only arrived in Spain after the Columbian exchange, so the red version is a fairly recent twist on the ancient soup.

holidays.name: National Microwave Oven Day
holidays.description: A toast, or rather a reheat, to the humble kitchen box that made leftovers, popcorn, and mug cakes possible in minutes. It's a day to appreciate the beep that signals your food is ready. It's also a day to remember all the times you forgot the cup of coffee inside.
holidays.origin: The observance honors the microwave oven, which grew out of radar technology research in the 1940s. Percy Spencer, an engineer at Raytheon, is credited with the discovery after a candy bar melted in his pocket near a radar device.
holidays.funFact: The first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, stood nearly six feet tall and weighed around 750 pounds. It was a far cry from the countertop models we know today.
